title: DWP's Universal Credit advances machine-learning model saved an estimated £4.4 million from 2022-23 to 2024-25
summary: The National Audit Office reports that DWP's model, in use since May 2022, flags high-risk advance requests for caseworker review, with estimated savings of £4.4 million and about three times the h...
account: The National Audit Office's report 'Tackling benefit overpayments due to fraud and error' (22 October 2025) states that since May 2022 the Department for Work & Pensions has used a machine learning model to flag potentially fraudulent claims for Universal Credit advances, saving an estimated £4.4 million from 2022-23 to 2024-25 by DWP's estimate, that the model scores new claims and refers those above a threshold to a caseworker while decisions are made by DWP staff, and that DWP cannot disaggregate the model's costs from wider spending on data analytics. The NAO reports DWP's finding that the model is around three times more effective at identifying fraud risk than a randomized control group sample, a median payment delay of one day for referred requests, and DWP's July 2025 fairness analysis for 2024-25 showing older claimants (age groups 45 to 54 and above) and non-UK nationals over-referred for review, with fairness analysis possible on only one of nine protected characteristics; four further models were in development. Civil Service World (Jim Dunton, 22 October 2025) reported the NAO's warnings on data infrastructure and quoted Transformation Minister Andrew Western saying that the one machine learning model has made the department significantly more effective. The date used is the NAO publication date.
purpose: Assess the fraud risk of Universal Credit advance requests and refer high-risk requests to a caseworker for review.
system: Universal Credit advances machine learning model
taxonomy_note: The £4.4 million saving is DWP's own estimate relayed by the NAO, with no cost figure to set against it. DWP's fairness analysis found over-referral of older and non-UK claimants, and the OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a related entry on bias in the UK benefits-fraud system (RSS headline, not fetched).

ratings.reason: The saving is an aggregate departmental estimate over three years, not an attributable outcome.
No outcome for claimants or taxpayers beyond the aggregate estimate is documented, and referred claimants bear an added evidence burden.

ai_role.statement: The NAO describes a model trained on historical fraud and error data that scores advance requests and refers those above a threshold; every payment decision is made by a caseworker, so the model's contribution is prioritization. Developer and deployer are the same public body (DWP); the NAO, an independent auditor, wrote the report.
